When the earth is shaken with its (final) quaking (﴿إِذَا زُلْزِلَتِ ٱلأَرْضُ﴾ "When the earth is shaken"), i.e., it is moved and convulsed. ﴿زِلْزَالَهَا﴾ ("its quaking") is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is attributed to the earth only for emphasis, as if to say: the quaking that befits it, given the magnitude of its body. ﴿وَأَخْرَجَتِ ٱلأَرْضُ أَثْقَالَهَا﴾ ("and the earth brings forth its burdens") means the dead who are within it, and this occurs at the second blast of the Trumpet (al-Ṣūr). It has been said that they are the treasures, but this is weak, because the bringing forth of treasures occurs at the time of the Dajjal (the Antichrist). ﴿وَقَالَ ٱلإِنسَانُ مَا لَهَا﴾ ("and man will say: 'What is wrong with it?'") means that he marvels at its condition. It may be understood to refer to mankind in general, or to the disbeliever in particular, since he is the one who, at that time, sees what he did not expect. ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا﴾ ("On that Day it will relate its news") is an expression for the terrors that occur upon it; it is therefore a metaphor (majāz) and a speaking through the tongue of its state (ḥadīth bi-lisān al-ḥāl). It has also been said that it is literal (ḥaqīqa): its testimony to people concerning what they did upon its surface. The verb tuḥaddithu (“it relates”) transitively takes two objects, of which the object has been omitted; the implied meaning is: it informs the creation of its news. Some of the muḥaddithūn (scholars of hadith) derived from the phrase "tuḥaddithu akhbārahā" that the statement of a narrator, "ḥaddathanā" (he related to us) and "akhbaranā" (he informed us), are the same. This sentence is the answer (jawāb) to "idhā zulzilat," and tuḥaddithu is the governing element (ʿāmil) of idhā. Yawma'idhin ("on that Day") is a substitute (badal) for idhā, and it is permissible that the governing element of idhā is a hidden verb, with tuḥaddithu governing yawma'idhin. ﴿بِأَنَّ رَبَّكَ أَوْحَىٰ لَهَا﴾ ("because your Lord has inspired it") — the bāʾ is causal (sababiyya), attached to tuḥaddithu, meaning: it relates because God has inspired it. It is also possible that "bi-anna Allāha awḥā lahā" is a substitute for "akhbārahā," and this is like your saying: "ḥaddathtu kadhā" and "ḥaddathtu bi-kadhā." The meaning in this case is: it relates the narrative of the revelation to it. This revelation may be inspiration (ilhām) or speech through the angels, and lahā here means ilayhā (to it). It has been said that the meaning is: He revealed to the angels on its account, but this is remote.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 99, verses 6–8:

﴿On that Day, people will emerge in scattered groups﴾ differing in their conditions. The singular of ashtat (scattered groups) is shatit. The "emergence" (sadr) of people is their departure from the place where they came to (wird). It has been said: the "coming to" (wird) is their burial in graves, and the "emergence" (sadr) is their standing up for resurrection. It has also been said: the "coming to" (wird) is their standing up for the gathering (hashr), and the "emergence" (sadr) is their departure toward Paradise or Hellfire. This is the more evident view. On that Day the difference between people's conditions becomes great, so their being scattered groups becomes manifest.

﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾. The mithqal is a weight, and dharra is a small ant. The "seeing" here is not seeing with the eye; it is an expression for recompense. Allah mentioned the atom's weight as a reminder of what is greater than it, by way of a fortiori reasoning, as if He said: whoever does little or much. This verse concerns believers, because the disbeliever is not recompensed in the Hereafter for his good deeds, since they are not accepted from him. The People of the Sunnah have used this verse as evidence that no believer abides forever in the Fire; for if he were to abide forever, he would not see a reward for his faith and for the good deeds he did. It is narrated from ʿĀʾishah that she gave away a single grape in charity, and when she was asked about that, she said: "How much of an atom's weight is in it?" A man heard this verse in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Allah is sufficient for me; I do not care to hear anything other than it."

﴿And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾. This applies in its generality to the disbeliever. As for believers, they are not recompensed for their sins except under six conditions: that their sins be major sins (kaba'ir), that they die without repenting from them, that they have no good deeds weightier in the balance than them, that no intercession be made for them, that they not be among those who deserved forgiveness through a deed, like the people of Badr, and that Allah not pardon them. For the believer who disobeys is under Allah's will: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him.
